note: Every table in public must appear here. A table in neither list fails supabase/tests/tenancy-tables.test.mjs, which is the point: a new table has to be classified at review time rather than discovered after Stage 4 makes it invisible.

buckets.tenant: Gets tenant_id in Stage 3 and a tenant isolation policy in Stage 4.
buckets.platform: Infrastructure and the global catalogue. Not owned by any tenant, so no tenant_id.
buckets.tenancy: The tenancy tables themselves. They define the boundary rather than sitting inside it: tenants.id IS the tenant and the other two name it directly, so none of them gains a tenant_id in Stage 3. They do get isolation policies in Stage 4.

identity.user_roles: Platform-level roles. Tenant-level role lives on tenant_members.
identity.users: One person, one account, across every tenant. What varies per tenant is the membership row, not the account.

platform.email_failures: Delivery diagnostics for the platform operator.
platform.products: The product catalogue, added in migration 0033. The same nine rows for every tenant, which is why it is not tenant-owned. Which products a given tenant has is tenant_products, in the tenancy bucket.
platform.rate_limits: Abuse control for the whole install, keyed by bucket and key. Not a tenant record.

tenancy.tenant_invitations: Pending invitations to join a business, added in migration 0047. Carries tenant_id already, so Stage 3 does not apply; it has an isolation-shaped policy of its own (admin of that tenant only). The invitee never reads it - they present a token to bos_accept_invitation, which is definer.
tenancy.tenant_members: Membership and the role held in it. The spine: role moves off users.primary_role onto this row, because admin is a fact about a person in a tenant.
tenancy.tenant_products: Which products a tenant has switched on, and the settings for each. Carries tenant_id already, so Stage 3 skips it; Stage 4 still gives it a policy.
tenancy.tenants: One row per business. Added in migration 0034.

uniqueConstraints.note: Computed from pg_index over the tenant-owned and tenancy tables, which covers unique INDEXES as well as unique constraints. It read pg_constraint until Stage 3, and so missed badges(slug) entirely: an index created with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX has no backing constraint but collides across tenants just the same. Every live one must appear in safe; scopedIn0036 is a record of what was replaced and is not checked against the database.

safe.badges(tenant_id,slug): Scoped by migration 0036. Was badges(slug), which a unique INDEX, not a constraint, which is why the first version of this audit never saw it. Two tenants would both want a first-event badge. Dropped and recreated with DROP INDEX rather than ALTER TABLE, despite being named badges_slug_key.
safe.campaigns(tenant_id,code): Scoped by migration 0036. Was campaigns(code), which a code is unique per business, not per platform.
safe.cashflow_months(tenant_id,month,scenario: Scoped by migration 0036. Was cashflow_months(month,scenario), which Every tenant has its own January.
safe.cities(tenant_id,name): Scoped by migration 0036. Was cities(name), which two businesses may both run a Chennai chapter.
safe.communities(tenant_id,slug): Scoped by migration 0036. Was communities(slug), which Slugs are per business.
safe.complaints(tenant_id,ref): Scoped by migration 0036. Was complaints(ref), which The C- series restarts per business.
safe.data_fields(tenant_id,table_name,column_: Scoped by migration 0036. Was data_fields(table_name,column_name), which Each tenant documents the same table for itself.
safe.email_templates(tenant_id,key): Scoped by migration 0036. Was email_templates(key), which Every tenant wants its own host_invite template.
safe.employee_module_access(tenant_id,user_id: Scoped by migration 0036. Was employee_module_access(user_id,section), which user_id is global, so one person in two tenants would get one grant row for both. The sharpest of these.
safe.employee_profiles(tenant_id,user_id): Scoped by migration 0036. Was employee_profiles(user_id), which One profile per person per tenant, not per person.
safe.events(tenant_id,slug): Scoped by migration 0036. Was events(slug), which Slugs are per business site.
safe.goals(tenant_id,code): Scoped by migration 0036. Was goals(code), which G-01 exists in every business.
safe.kpi_values(tenant_id,kpi_id,period): Scoped by migration 0036. Was kpi_values(kpi_id,period), which kpi_id is tenant-owned so this is nearly safe, but the pair is cheap to extend and keeps the index aligned with every read.
safe.membership_plans(tenant_id,tier): Scoped by migration 0036. Was membership_plans(tier), which Each business defines its own Gold.
safe.newsletter_subscribers(tenant_id,email): Scoped by migration 0036. Was newsletter_subscribers(email), which One address may subscribe to two businesses.
safe.promo_codes(tenant_id,code): Scoped by migration 0036. Was promo_codes(code), which LAUNCH50 belongs to whoever issued it.
safe.registrations(ticket_code): Deliberately global. The door scanner looks a ticket up by code alone, so codes must not repeat across tenants.
safe.reviews(tenant_id,period_type,period_sta: Scoped by migration 0036. Was reviews(period_type,period_start), which One review per period per business.
safe.risks(tenant_id,code): Scoped by migration 0036. Was risks(code), which R-01 exists in every register.
safe.sop_acknowledgements(version_id,user_id): version_id is tenant-owned, which scopes the pair.
safe.sop_documents(tenant_id,code): Scoped by migration 0036. Was sop_documents(code), which SOP codes are per business.
safe.tasks(tenant_id,code): Scoped by migration 0036. Was tasks(code), which T-001 exists in every backlog.
safe.tenant_invitations(tenant_id,email): Includes tenant_id by construction: one invitation per address per business.
safe.tenant_members(tenant_id,user_id): Includes tenant_id by construction, which is what lets one person belong to two tenants.
safe.tenants(slug): Deliberately global. A slug identifies a tenant across the whole platform, so this is one of the few unique constraints that must NOT be scoped to a tenant.
safe.user_badges(user_id,badge_id): badge_id is tenant-owned, which scopes the pair.
safe.workstreams(tenant_id,key): Scoped by migration 0036. Was workstreams(key), which Keys are per business.

partialIndexesNotListed.payments(provider,provider_ref) where pr: Left global on purpose. A Razorpay payment id is unique worldwide, so scoping it to a tenant would allow the same provider reference to be recorded twice.
partialIndexesNotListed.post_reports(post_id,reporter_id) where: post_id is tenant-owned, which scopes the pair.
partialIndexesNotListed.post_reports(comment_id,reporter_id) whe: comment_id is tenant-owned, which scopes the pair.
partialIndexesNotListed.tenants(is_default) where is_default: Platform-level by design: at most one default tenant across the whole install.
partialIndexesNotListed._note: The guard skips partial unique indexes, because a predicate changes what the index means and each needs reading rather than listing. These four were read; if a fifth appears, it belongs here with a reason.

forceRlsNote: MEASURED IN PRODUCTION, 6 October 2026: postgres=bypasses, service_role=bypasses, authenticated=subject, anon=subject. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is therefore worthless in this project and will never be applied. It removes the OWNERSHIP exemption; it does not touch the BYPASSRLS role attribute. public tables are owned by postgres, which carries BYPASSRLS, so the owner - and every SECURITY DEFINER function running as the owner - bypasses RLS whether FORCE is set or not. This also corrects the reason given in migration 0037 for leaving FORCE out. The concern there was that FORCE would break all 77 definer functions, which is true of a non-superuser owner without BYPASSRLS and was demonstrated in a controlled test; it is NOT true here, because they keep bypassing via the role attribute. The real reason is simpler: it would change nothing. The consequence is the important part. The owner hole cannot be closed by any database-level switch. It can only be closed inside each function body, which makes the Stage 5 audit of the 77 definer functions the single control standing between one tenant and another. The architecture document named FORCE as part of that control; it is not.
isolation: Stage 4 added one RESTRICTIVE policy named 'tenant isolation' to each of the 87 tenant-owned tables, scoped to authenticated and anon, with both USING and WITH CHECK against bos_request_tenant(). Restrictive because Postgres OR-s permissive policies: an ordinary policy saying 'or the row is in your tenant' would have widened access past the existing per-user rules instead of narrowing it. The tenancy tables are excluded on purpose - reading tenant_members across tenants is how switching works.
